analysis.one_liner: Creates a voluntary Medicare prescription drug benefit for seniors and disabled beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in June 2000, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a prescription drug benefit to Medicare, open to every senior and disabled beneficiary, with the government paying half of drug costs up to a yearly limit and everything above a high stop-loss amount. Premiums would be split between enrollees and the Treasury, and low-income beneficiaries would get their premiums and copays covered through Medicaid with the federal government picking up the full cost. The benefit would be administered through private contractors called "benefit managers" rather than by Medicare itself, and the government would be barred from negotiating drug prices or setting formularies.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries without drug coverage — roughly a third of seniors at the time — who would gain insurance against high pharmacy bills, with the strongest protection going to low-income beneficiaries whose premiums and cost-sharing would be fully covered. Retiree plan sponsors, pharmacy benefit managers, pharmacies, and drug makers would also gain new revenue streams.

how_it_helps.text: Every Medicare beneficiary would be eligible to enroll, and the program would pay 50% of the price of covered prescriptions up to an annual limit ($2,000 in 2002-2003, rising to $5,000 by 2008) and 100% of costs above a stop-loss amount ($5,000 in 2002). [S2] [S3]
A prescribed drug must be covered even if it is not on the benefit manager's formulary, when a health care professional certifies it is medically necessary. [S3]
Low-income beneficiaries under 150% of the poverty line would have premiums and drug cost-sharing paid through Medicaid, with the federal government matching 100% of that cost-sharing. [S2] [S3]
Premiums would be deducted from Social Security checks the same way Medicare Part B premiums are, simplifying enrollment for beneficiaries. [S3]

Employers who keep offering retiree drug coverage would receive a subsidy equal to two-thirds of the monthly enrollee premium for each covered retiree, discouraging employers from dropping retiree drug plans. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would appropriate contributions matching half of enrollee premiums (two-thirds of the premium for retirees whose former employers pay); enrollees, who would pay the other half of the premium; and pharmacies and drug makers, whose prices would be set by benefit managers under contract terms.

drawbacks.text: The benefit has a gap: after paying 50% of costs up to the initial limit ($2,000 in 2002-2003), the enrollee pays 100% of drug costs alone until spending reaches the $5,000 stop-loss, leaving heavy users of medicines with thousands of dollars in uncovered costs. [S3]

The bill contains a noninterference clause stating that nothing in it authorizes the government to set a formulary, establish a price structure, or interfere with the competitive provision of the benefit — Medicare would have no leverage over drug prices. [S3]

The bill expressly makes Medicaid drug price rebates unavailable for drugs purchased through the Medicare buy-in, so the government would pay negotiated-retail prices rather than the discounted prices Medicaid obtains. [S3]

Prices for covered drugs set by benefit managers are not subject to administrative or judicial review, and dispensing fees to pharmacies are not guaranteed, concentrating pricing power in private middlemen. [S3]
Benefit managers may propose higher government cost-sharing for formulary and mail-order drugs, steering beneficiaries toward channels the manager favors. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real drug benefit for people who had none, with unusually strong low-income protections, but deliberately weak on cost control: the design routes public money through private benefit managers, forbids Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and excludes Medicaid-style rebates, so taxpayers and enrollees would pay more per prescription than a government-administered benefit likely would.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means and Commerce committees after a June 2000 introduction, was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on June 8, 2000, joined by 12 colleagues as original cosponsors. [S3] [S5]
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total. [S4]
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Commerce Committee on the day of introduction. [S5]
On June 19, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and the record shows no markup, vote, or floor action afterward. [S5]
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill still in committee. [S1]

Prescription drug coverage for Medicare beneficiaries was a major issue in the 2000 election year, and competing drug benefit plans were advanced by both parties; no Medicare drug bill became law that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained coverage — Medicare beneficiaries without drug benefits went another three years without one. Drug makers and pharmacy benefit managers were better off because no federal drug program, even one with private administration and no price negotiation, moved that year.

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 17 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Ways and Means and Commerce committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the two committees of referral (106th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; the record shows no committee action after the June 19, 2000 subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: In the 2000 election year, advanced the majority's own competing Medicare drug proposals and never brought this Democratic bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats; the bill died in committees controlled by the Republican majority without a recorded vote, though both parties publicly favored some form of Medicare drug benefit in 2000.

industries.note: The bill makes private benefit managers, under contract with the Office of Personnel Management, the permanent channel for administering the entire benefit, and bars the government from setting formularies or prices. Medicare beneficiaries gain coverage, but the middlemen who price claims and control formularies are locked in rather than bypassed.

A new federal drug benefit would expand demand for prescriptions, while the bill's noninterference clause bars Medicare from negotiating prices or setting formularies, and it expressly excludes Medicaid-style price rebates for drugs bought through the program. The industry's gain would come at the cost of higher public and out-of-pocket prices.

An incentive program would pay sponsors two-thirds of the monthly premium for each retiree kept on a company drug plan, subsidizing an employer benefit that might otherwise be cut. Retirees keep their coverage; taxpayers fund the subsidy.

Any qualifying pharmacy could participate, expanding access, but benefit managers would set the price schedule and could offer preferential terms to favored pharmacies, and dispensing fees are not guaranteed.
Private Medicare plans would be paid from the new Prescription Drug Insurance Account to offer part D benefits to their enrollees, adding a federal revenue stream for the private plan industry.
